trainings_new.title: Our eight charitable activities
trainings_new.description: What we are registered to do, how each activity works in practice, and how to talk about it.

body.summary: The eight activities we described to the CRA when we applied for charitable status, what each one looks like in practice, and how to talk about our work.

blocks.text: When Welfare Avenue applied for charitable status, we described our work to the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) as eight charitable activities. They are the backbone of everything we do: every serving, drive, workshop and partnership should trace back to at least one of them.
Our charitable purposes are the **relief of poverty** and the **advancement of education**. The eight activities are how we carry out those purposes, day to day.

Welfare Avenue is a youth-powered non-profit dedicated to fighting food insecurity and poverty through direct community action, delivering meals and essential support directly to people where they are.

blocks.note: From our 2026 brand guide and recent grant applications.

blocks.text: Tap an activity to open it. Each one has a purpose, the way we carry it out, and the teams involved.

items.sum: Building relationships with organizations, businesses and schools that share our mission, so we reach more people and pool resources.
how: Find organizations working on poverty, food security and inclusion, and learn about their impact.
Reach out, meet, and present our mission and current activities.
Write tailored partnership and sponsorship proposals with clear roles and shared projects.
Run the joint projects, then review the results together and adjust.
items.teams: Outreach finds and grows partners and sponsors, Marketing promotes, Operations runs the volunteer base and equipment, Finance tracks sponsorship and campaign money, and the executive team makes sure every partnership fits the mission.
items.extra: As a youth-powered organization, outreach also builds our volunteer base through schools, student associations and clubs.

items.sum: Relieving poverty by getting clothing, hygiene products and other essentials to people who need them, and connecting them with services.
how: Run donation drives with supermarkets, schools, colleges and companies.
Sort, store and distribute what comes in, with volunteers at every step.
Connect people with mental health, employment, housing and shelter resources through our network.
Gather feedback after each drive to make the next one better.
items.teams: Operations runs collection and distribution, Outreach brings in organizations and students, Marketing invites the community to contribute, and Finance tracks what we spend.

items.sum: Addressing food insecurity with free meals at our Sunday servings.
how: Fundraise for food and receive food donations.
Plan meals with Canada's Food Guide in mind: fresh, balanced and mostly plant-based.
Coordinate volunteer cooks, drivers and servers through the volunteering manager.
Serve with care: safely, respectfully and on time.
items.teams: Operations plans each serving, the recipes and the food, Finance tracks food spending and budgets, Marketing raises awareness of food insecurity, and Outreach finds funding for meals.

items.sum: Addressing isolation by making our servings and events places where people feel welcome and connected.
how: Organize free community events, indoors and outdoors, where everyone can take part.
Put the proceeds of paid events back into food, hygiene supplies and clothing.
Talk with the people we serve, one on one and in groups, to understand their needs and build real connection.
Help young people understand homelessness and reduce stigma.
items.teams: Operations makes each serving a place for real connection, Outreach and Marketing raise awareness of isolation, and Finance keeps money available for community events.

items.sum: Helping people meet their basic needs by knowing what support exists and how to reach it.
how: Make space for open conversation at servings to learn what people need, including dietary needs and preferences.
Bring in information from partner organizations on mental health, shelters, housing and employment training.
Turn it into clear infographics, factsheets and brochures that we share at servings.
items.teams: Operations makes sure people know where we will be and what is available, Marketing shows why access matters, and Outreach shares what people tell us they need.

items.sum: Engaging students and young people to take action on poverty and homelessness.
how: Network at schools such as McGill, Concordia, Dawson and Vanier.
Run campus events like bake sales and student gatherings to raise awareness, volunteers and donations.
Offer volunteer roles and run workshops that encourage civic engagement.
items.teams: Outreach works with schools and clubs, Operations sets new student volunteers up, and Marketing reaches students online.

items.sum: Joining forces with non-profits and charities on the issues that affect the people we serve.
how: Network with local organizations, charities and community workers.
Take part in advisory work on poverty, such as Campaign 2000 advisory meetings.
Attend events that highlight these issues, such as Disability Without Poverty and Dignity for All.
items.teams: Outreach connects with other charities, Operations runs joint volunteer events, and Marketing supports partners online.

items.t: A voice for the people we serve
items.sum: Working with people who share our concern, and bringing the lived experience of the people we serve into the conversation.
how: Attend forums and conferences on poverty and homelessness in Canada.
Listen closely through conversations and feedback surveys, and learn the barriers people face.
Use what we learn to shape our services and to raise awareness on social media.
items.teams: Outreach attends forums and conferences, Operations gathers feedback at servings, Marketing amplifies the voices of the people we serve, and the executive team keeps everyone coordinated.

blocks.text: Team names are as written in our submission. They map onto today's departments on the Hub.
Our 2026 brand guide describes the same work as four pillars. Here is how the eight activities feed them.

items.d: Consistent, well-coordinated food distribution, using the meal as a trust-building first step toward long-term reintegration.
Seasonal clothing, hygiene essentials and basic amenities, always offered with respect and solidarity.
Pop-ups, creative arts and recreational sports that break down barriers and build belonging.
Bridging street-level trust with housing, mental health and employment networks across our partners.

blocks.t: And the energy behind all four
blocks.text: Activities 6 and 8 are why we call ourselves youth-powered: young leaders mobilizing their communities, and a voice for the people we serve.
Our submission names **Place Émilie-Gamelin** (1500 rue Berri, by Berri-UQAM) as our main serving location, with a storage unit in Parc-Extension for the tents, tables and serving equipment.
Schools and campuses host much of our outreach, youth and education work: LaurenHill Academy, Vanier College, McGill, Dawson and Concordia.
Today we work in Montreal and Toronto, in parks, shelters and other community spaces.
The volunteering manager has the details of the next serving: date, place, roster and checklist. Take its page tour to see how it works.

chapters.t: Who we serve, and how we say it

blocks.text: We serve people experiencing homelessness or housing instability, low-income individuals and families, and anyone facing food insecurity. Support is based on need: people self-identify, or a partner organization refers them.
The words we use matter. If we call it the wrong word, someone reading gets the wrong image of what we do.

items: The people we serve, community, support
Support, dignity, connection, safety
Food as a starting point, refer, reintegrate
Youth-powered, professional, a movement
Collaborate, ecosystem, partnership
The homeless, beneficiaries, people in need
Pity, saving people, feeling sorry
Feed people, hand out food
Student club, just volunteers, a small project
We do everything, we're the only ones

blocks.text: Formal filings, like our CRA forms, use the word beneficiaries because it is the legal term. Everywhere else, we say the people we serve.
Advancing education is part of our charitable purpose, not an extra. We help our community understand food insecurity, isolation and access to resources, and invite them to act.

items: Workshops and presentations in schools, from LaurenHill Academy to Concordia.
Conferences such as Apathy is Boring, and Force Avenir, where we were selected in the Mutual Aid, Peace and Justice category.
Research and knowledge sharing: infographics, factsheets and information letters.
Social media that shows homelessness is about belonging and dignity, not only basic necessities.
Recruiting people who care about their community, and helping them grow professionally.

items.t: Tie your work to an activity
items.d: When you plan an event, a post or a partnership, know which activity it serves. It makes reports, grant applications and our annual return stronger.
If an idea does not clearly fit one of the eight activities or our purposes, check with the executive team before committing time or money.
Say the people we serve, and lead with dignity.
Log servings, volunteers and outcomes in the Hub so the numbers are ready when a funder or the CRA asks.

blocks.d: Our 8 Charitable Activities, the training copy of our submission to the CRA Charities Directorate.

questions.q: What are our two charitable purposes?
a: Relief of poverty and advancement of education
questions.why: Everything we do serves the relief of poverty and the advancement of education.

questions.q: Our Sunday servings mainly carry out which activity?
questions.why: Free, healthy meals address food insecurity. Servings touch other activities too, like community and belonging.

a: With Canada's Food Guide in mind: fresh, balanced and mostly plant-based
questions.why: Healthy meals are part of dignity: fresh ingredients, balanced and mostly plant-based.

questions.q: Which activity is about making servings and events places of belonging?
questions.why: Isolation is as real as hunger. Activity 4 is about welcome, conversation and connection.

questions.q: How do we refer to the people who come to our servings?
questions.why: We lead with the person, not their circumstance. Beneficiary is only the legal term in formal filings.

questions.q: You have an idea for a project that does not clearly fit any of the eight activities. What do you do?
a: Check with the executive team before committing time or money
questions.why: Our resources must go to our charitable purposes. A quick check keeps us compliant and often sharpens the idea.

trainings_new.title: Our partners and how we work with them
trainings_new.description: Partners, sponsors and collaborators, who we work with today, and how a partnership comes together.

body.summary: Why we partner, the difference between partners, sponsors and collaborators, who we work with today, and how a partnership comes together.

blocks.text: Welfare Avenue does not try to do everything itself. We complement the services that already exist and connect people with the right support. Partners make that possible.
Collaboration is the default. Until we build a larger audience, most events run with a partner org that shares the planning load.

items.d: Combining strengths, resources and expertise lets us reach more people, more effectively.
Programs shaped with partners reflect the communities we serve.
Co-created programs draw on shared knowledge and experience.
Kitchens, halls, equipment and networks, without duplicating effort.
Joint communication amplifies both missions.

blocks.text: Three words, three different relationships. Using the right one keeps our records, reports and thank-yous accurate.

items.d: An organization we work with toward a shared goal, through joint programs or initiatives. Formalized in writing: an MOU or a project agreement.
items.e: DESTA Black Community Network (community kitchen and a joint grant application), Union United Church (kitchen space).

items.d: A person, business or organization that gives money or in-kind support, and gets recognition in return.
items.e: VCSA (has funded our club since the beginning), Sportira (jerseys and pinnies), Poulet Rouge (Flag Football).

items.d: An organization that joins us for an event or initiative, without a formal agreement.
items.e: Student clubs and companies that join a serving or co-host a fundraiser.

blocks.text: Collaborators often become partners or sponsors. Every good event is the start of a relationship, so log it.

blocks.d: Every organization, its status, point of contact, notes and completed goals.

blocks.text: Every organization in the sheet has a status. Moving a relationship forward is a team effort, so keep it current.

items.d: Someone to contact. Pick an owner and a first step.
Conversations are happening. Agree on a first joint project.
We have worked together and plan to keep going.

No reply, or not interested. Note why, and move on.
The goals, the programs or events involved, and the impact we expect for the people we serve.
Who coordinates, who handles volunteers, logistics, communications and reporting. One point of contact on each side.
Facilities, equipment, volunteers, materials and timelines, plus any budget or in-kind contributions.
An MOU or project agreement covering commitments, liability, safeguarding, branding and reporting.
Clear measures, regular check-ins, and feedback from partners, volunteers and the people we serve.
How good work continues, and how to end a partnership responsibly if it needs to.

blocks.text: Three models give us a flexible starting point, from our community kitchen partnership plan:

items.d: A partner provides a space, like a certified kitchen, on a predictable schedule. We bring the volunteers, food and supplies.
We design and deliver a program together, sharing the work and the credit.
A short trial with clear goals. Then we decide together what comes next.

chapters.t: What we offer, what we ask

items: A dedicated, diverse volunteer network
Experience designing and delivering programs
A strong community presence
Promotion on our channels, and co-branding
Alignment with our mission and values
Resources: space, expertise, networks or funding
A collaborative spirit and open communication
Active support for delivery and outreach

blocks.text: And the principles we hold ourselves to:

items.d: Every partner gets real value, and is treated fairly.
Open communication and responsible use of every resource.
Regular, consistent updates build trust.
Everyone is treated with dignity and respect, and partners follow safeguarding practices.
Measurable outcomes for the communities we serve.
Before contacting an organization, look it up in the Partner Relations sheet. Someone may already own the relationship.
The Partnership Email Templates cover pharmacies, clothing charities and thrift stores, food suppliers and restaurants, and other non-profits.
Update the status, point of contact, notes and completed goals after each conversation.
Anything involving money, logos or a formal agreement goes through your lead and the executive team.

items.t: Bring it back to the Hub
items.d: Record outcomes on your team page, and ask Marketing through Requests for co-branded posts.

questions.q: A company gives us $500 and we put their logo on our event banner. What is that relationship?
questions.why: Sponsors give money or in-kind support and get recognition in return.

questions.q: A student club joins one of our Sunday servings, with no formal agreement. What is that?
questions.why: Collaborators join events or initiatives without a formal agreement, and often grow into partners.

questions.q: Before emailing an organization about working together, what comes first?
a: Check the Partner Relations sheet for an existing relationship
Post about it on social media
questions.why: Someone may already own the relationship. The sheet also shows the history, so your email starts in the right place.

questions.q: What formalizes a partnership's roles, liability, safeguarding and branding?
questions.why: Partnerships are formalized in writing, with roles, responsibilities and expectations agreed up front.

questions.q: A relationship is marked Collaborated but dormant. What is the best move?
questions.why: We have worked together before. A clear, specific ask is the best way to restart.

questions.q: Which model fits using a partner's certified kitchen on a predictable schedule?
questions.why: In a host arrangement the partner provides the space; we bring the volunteers, food and supplies.

module7:
The Training academy starts with your onboarding: your onboarding plan week by week, the Hub first steps and the policies to sign. Below it: your level and progress, what is up next, learning paths with a certificate at the end, a guided tour for every page of the Hub, and the full library of videos, lessons and documents. Open anything and it fills the screen: watch, read or take the quiz, then mark it complete. Certificates and badges show on your profile. HR manages onboarding and assigns trainings from the HR centre.

Try it: take the tour of the academy itself, then one page tour.

Done when: you know where your onboarding, your assigned trainings and the page tours live.
